description: Complexity classes + reductions decomposed. P, NP, NP-complete, NP-hard, co-NP, PSPACE, EXP. Reductions as the tool for showing relative hardness. Famous problems + their classifications. P vs NP as the central open question.

sub_mechanisms.name: P_polynomial_time
sub_mechanisms.definition: Decision problems solvable by a deterministic Turing machine in time O(n^k) for some constant k.
sub_mechanisms.why: Captures 'efficiently solvable in theory'. Sorting, primality (AKS), shortest paths, max-flow all in P. Boundary between tractable and intractable in standard CS theory.

sub_mechanisms.name: NP_polynomial_verifiable
sub_mechanisms.definition: Decision problems where a YES instance admits a polynomial-time-checkable certificate. Equivalent: solvable by nondeterministic Turing machine in polynomial time.
sub_mechanisms.why: P ⊆ NP (anything solvable is verifiable: solve it). Whether the reverse holds is the open P vs NP question. Most 'interesting' hard problems live in NP.

sub_mechanisms.name: polynomial_reduction
sub_mechanisms.definition: Problem A reduces to B (A ≤_p B) if there's a polynomial-time function transforming A-instances to B-instances preserving YES/NO.
sub_mechanisms.why: If B is in P and A ≤_p B, then A is in P. Reductions transfer tractability + hardness. The relation underlies all complexity-class definitions.

sub_mechanisms.name: NP_complete_definition
sub_mechanisms.definition: L is NP-complete iff (1) L ∈ NP and (2) every L' ∈ NP polynomially reduces to L. The 'hardest' problems in NP.
sub_mechanisms.why: If any NP-complete problem is in P, then P = NP. They're all equivalent in difficulty. The famous Karp 21 problems established the class's breadth.

sub_mechanisms.name: Cook_Levin_theorem
sub_mechanisms.definition: SAT is NP-complete (Cook 1971, Levin 1973 independently). Every NP problem reduces to SAT.
sub_mechanisms.why: Foundational: gives the first NP-complete problem. All other NP-completeness proofs reduce from SAT (or from problems known to be reducible from SAT). Without Cook-Levin, NP-completeness theory wouldn't exist.

sub_mechanisms.name: 3_SAT_NP_complete
sub_mechanisms.definition: Boolean satisfiability with clauses restricted to 3 literals each. Reduced from general SAT in polynomial time.
sub_mechanisms.why: The 'simplest' NP-complete problem. Many reductions start from 3-SAT because clause structure is regular. Used to prove NP-completeness of graph problems, scheduling, etc.

sub_mechanisms.name: NP_hard_definition
sub_mechanisms.definition: L is NP-hard if every NP problem reduces to L. L need not be in NP itself (could be even harder, e.g., undecidable).
sub_mechanisms.why: NP-complete = NP-hard + in NP. Many optimisation problems are NP-hard but not in NP (because they're not decision problems). 'NP-hard' is the weaker / more general statement.

sub_mechanisms.name: coNP_class
sub_mechanisms.definition: Decision problems where a NO instance admits a polynomial-time-checkable certificate. The complement of NP.
sub_mechanisms.why: TAUT (Boolean tautology) is coNP-complete. Whether NP = coNP is another open question (consequence: P = NP iff NP = coNP if either holds). Captures asymmetry in verification: easy to verify YES vs easy to verify NO.

sub_mechanisms.name: PSPACE_class
sub_mechanisms.definition: Problems solvable using polynomial space (any amount of time). PSPACE ⊇ NP ∪ coNP.
sub_mechanisms.why: Game-playing problems (chess, go on n×n board), quantified Boolean formula. PSPACE-complete is even harder than NP-complete (PSPACE ⊇ NP). The space hierarchy theorem makes class separation precise.

sub_mechanisms.name: approximation_algorithm
sub_mechanisms.definition: Polynomial-time algorithm producing a solution within factor α of optimal. For TSP metric: 1.5-approximation (Christofides).
sub_mechanisms.why: When exact NP-hard solutions are intractable, approximations are. Approximation ratio is the worst-case ratio (algorithm value / optimal value). PCP theorem characterises which problems are approximable.

sub_mechanisms.name: P_vs_NP_open_question
sub_mechanisms.definition: Is P = NP? Open since 1971. Most theoretical computer scientists believe P ≠ NP.
sub_mechanisms.why: Central question of theoretical CS. P = NP would mean all NP problems efficiently solvable; would break cryptography. Would also mean P = NP-complete, so any NP-complete algorithm gives all of them.

sub_mechanisms.name: FPT_fixed_parameter_tractable
sub_mechanisms.definition: Problem is FPT if solvable in O(f(k) · n^c) where k is some parameter, c is constant, f is arbitrary (e.g., exponential).
sub_mechanisms.why: Some NP-hard problems are tractable when a parameter is small. Vertex cover is FPT in cover size; TSP is FPT in treewidth. Parameterised complexity is a finer-grained classification within NP-hardness.

derivation_rules.name: polynomial_reductions_compose
derivation_rules.why: Polynomial × polynomial = polynomial. Reductions chain transitively. This is what makes NP-completeness proofs by chaining work: once you have one NP-complete problem, you reduce it to others.

derivation_rules.name: any_NP_complete_in_P_implies_P_equals_NP
if: any NP-complete problem is in P
derivation_rules.why: If L is NP-complete in P, then for any L' in NP: L' ≤_p L. L solvable in polynomial time means L' is. Therefore NP ⊆ P. Combined with P ⊆ NP: P = NP. The single-problem path to a resolution.

derivation_rules.name: Cook_Levin_grounds_NP_completeness
if: we want to prove problem L is NP-complete
then: the standard approach is to show L ∈ NP and some NP-complete problem reduces to L
derivation_rules.why: Without Cook-Levin's seed (SAT is NP-complete), we'd have no starting problem. The standard proof technique reduces FROM a known NP-complete problem (typically 3-SAT or vertex cover) TO the target. Karp's 21 problems established the rich web of reductions.

derivation_rules.name: NP_hard_problems_admit_approximation_or_FPT
then: practical approaches are approximation, heuristic, or parameterised algorithms
derivation_rules.why: Exact polynomial algorithm probably doesn't exist (P ≠ NP). Practical paths: approximation (within α of optimal), heuristics (no guarantee but good in practice), FPT (polynomial when a parameter is small). Choice depends on problem structure.

derivation_rules.name: PCP_theorem_inapproximability
then: some NP-hard problems are NP-hard to approximate within any constant factor
derivation_rules.why: PCP (Probabilistically Checkable Proofs) gives a robust characterisation of NP that translates to inapproximability. MAX-3SAT is NP-hard to approximate within 7/8 + ε. Without PCP, we'd have no general theory of approximation hardness.
